objective: Screen for suicide and homicide risk, and keep a patient at risk safe in the department

sources.cite: Emergency nursing certification exam content outline (effective July 2026), category 6: Mental Health Emergencies (8.67% of the exam), which lists suicide and homicide risk
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/cen.ts), which read the outline 2026-11-14; the objective title is the course's own.

sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

brief.situation: Daniel Ruiz, 41 (a fictional patient), came to the emergency department at 02:10 with a racing heart and no sleep for four nights. His ECG and labs are back and the emergency physician has found no cardiac cause. At triage he said, 'I just need something to sleep. I can't keep doing this.' The department screens every patient for suicide risk with a validated tool, and his screen was not done at triage because he went straight to a monitored bed. His sister drove him and is in the waiting room. You are his emergency nurse; the physician is with a trauma patient for the next while. You have about 40 minutes before the morning rush.
handover: Triage: palpitations and insomnia; vital signs now in range; 'I can't keep doing this.' Suicide risk screen not yet done.
Department policy: a positive screen goes to the emergency physician at once; an acute positive is kept in sight at all times in the safe room until an emergency behavioral health evaluation.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Daniel answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. What he tells you depends on the trust you have built.
Your time with him ends at 40 minutes. Afterward you write a short risk formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.note: About 40 minutes of one emergency nurse's time with one patient before the morning rush (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: Open: 'Your heart tests look okay. How are you doing right now?'

effects.log: You sit at eye level, give him the test results and ask how he is doing.

effects.finding: "Okay is a strong word. I haven't slept since Thursday." He rubs his face.

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: He nods slowly. "Yeah. That's it exactly."

normalize.label: Normalize: 'We ask everyone some questions about safety. It matters.'

effects.log: You explain that the department asks every patient about suicide and that it is safe to answer honestly.

effects.finding: He lets out a breath. "Okay. Go ahead."

screen.label: Screen with the NIMH Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (the four questions)
screen.why: He has answered; go on to the follow-up questions.

effects.log: You ask the four screening questions directly: wishing he were dead, feeling his family would be better off, thoughts of killing himself this past week, and any past attempt.

then.finding: A long pause. "Yes to the first three. Every night this week. Never tried before."

then.log: Positive screen: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden and suicidal thoughts this week; no past attempt.

then.finding: "No. I'm just tired. Can I get something to sleep?" (Not yet enough trust to answer honestly.)

askNow.label: Ask the acuity question: thoughts of killing himself right now?
askNow.available: not talking and (siKnown and not acuteAsked)
askNow.why: Screen first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether he is having thoughts of killing himself right now.

effects.finding: "Right now? Yes. Not here. But yes."

askPlan.label: Ask whether he has thought about how, or made a plan (do not ask for details)
askPlan.available: not talking and (siKnown and not planAsked)
askPlan.why: Screen first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether he has thought about how he would do it, or made a plan, without asking him to describe it.

effects.finding: "I've thought about how. I'm not going to say it." He says he has a plan.

askIntent.label: Ask about intent to act
askIntent.available: not talking and (siKnown and not intentAsked)
askIntent.why: Screen first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether he intends to act on the thoughts.

effects.finding: "Some nights I think I would. Tonight I came here instead."

askBehavior.label: Ask about preparation or steps taken toward ending his life
askBehavior.available: not talking and (siKnown and not behaviorAsked)
askBehavior.why: Screen first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether he has done anything to prepare.

effects.finding: "I wrote letters to my kids on Sunday." Preparatory behavior this week.

askAccess.label: Ask whether what he has thought of is within reach, here or at home
askAccess.available: not talking and (siKnown and not accessAsked)
askAccess.why: Screen first (or you have asked this).

effects.log: You ask whether he has access to what he has thought of, with him or at home.

effects.finding: "At home. Not on me." He looks at his jacket on the chair.

askSupports.label: Ask what keeps him going and who supports him

effects.log: You ask what keeps him going and who he leans on.

effects.finding: "My kids. Ten and twelve. My sister Lucia, she drove me." His voice breaks on the kids.

safeRoom.label: Move him to the department's safe room, checked and cleared under the environmental risk policy
safeRoom.available: not talking and (siKnown and not envSafe)

effects.log: You move him to the safe room, which has been checked and cleared of anything that could be used for self-harm, and explain why.

belongings.label: Check and store his belongings with security, as the policy sets out, explaining why
belongings.available: not talking and (siKnown and not belongingsSafe)

effects.log: With a security officer, you explain the policy, check his belongings and store them outside the room.

effects.finding: He hands over his jacket. "You'll give it back?" "Yes, when you go home."

notifyMd.label: Tell the emergency physician now: acute positive screen (SBAR)
notifyMd.available: not talking and (siKnown and not notified)

effects.log: You step to the doorway, keeping him in view, and give the physician an SBAR: acute positive screen, plan, some intent, letters written.

effects.finding: The physician comes between cases, sees him briefly and orders an emergency behavioral health evaluation; he is not to leave before it.

pageBh.label: Page the behavioral health evaluator, as ordered, and give a verbal handoff
pageBh.available: not talking and (notified and not evalPaged)

effects.log: You page the behavioral health evaluator and hand off what he told you, the screen and the observation level.

effects.finding: The evaluator will be there within the hour and asks you to keep him on constant observation until then.

sister.label: With his consent, bring his sister Lucia in
sister.available: not talking and (supportsAsked and not familyIn)
sister.why: Ask who supports him first (or done).

effects.log: You ask whether he wants Lucia with him; he nods, and you bring her in.

effects.finding: Lucia takes his hand. "I'm not going anywhere."

leaveAlone.label: Step out to find the physician, leaving him alone for a few minutes

effects.log: You leave the room to find the physician, and he is alone for several minutes.

effects.finding: When you come back he is standing with his jacket on. "I'm going home."

effects.log: A patient with a positive screen was left alone and out of sight.

contract.label: Ask him to promise he will not hurt himself

effects.log: You ask him to promise he will not hurt himself tonight.
A promise is not a safety measure and has no evidence of protecting anyone.
You set his observation level.

then.finding: A patient safety attendant sits by the open door, in sight of him at all times.
A tech will look in every 15 minutes.

formulation.question: Write your risk formulation for Daniel: his risk level and why (what the screen and your follow-up questions showed, risk and protective factors), and what you put in place.

parts.label: Risk level and reasons
parts.criteria: Names an acute positive screen (imminent risk): suicidal thoughts right now, a plan, some intent, letters written this week, four nights without sleep; protective: his children, his sister, came in for help.
parts.modelAnswer: Acute positive: thoughts of killing himself right now, a plan he would not describe, some intent on recent nights and letters to his children this week. Protective factors are his children, his sister and that he came in. He cannot leave before an emergency behavioral health evaluation.

parts.label: What was put in place
parts.criteria: Names constant observation, the safe room, belongings stored per policy, the physician told at once and the evaluator paged with a handoff.
parts.modelAnswer: Constant observation by an attendant, the cleared safe room, his belongings stored with security, his sister with him by his choice, the physician told at once and the evaluator paged with a verbal handoff.

expertPath.text: Sit at eye level, reflect, normalize the questions, then screen with the four questions.
Ask the acuity question; then plan, intent and preparation, without asking for details; ask about access and supports.

safe.headline: Good: safe until the evaluation
safe.body: You screened early, asked the acuity question, followed up directly without asking for details, kept him in sight in a cleared room and got the physician and evaluator involved.

safeGaps.headline: Safe for now, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Daniel stayed, but the criteria below show what was late or missing.

unsafe.headline: Left at foreseeable risk
unsafe.body: A statement like his calls for the screen, the acuity question, constant observation and an evaluation before he leaves. The most useful kind of run to learn from.

walkout.headline: The conversation broke
walkout.body: False reassurance and advice closed him down before the screen. Reflection and calm, direct questions keep a patient talking.

scoring.modelReasoning: A statement like 'I can't keep doing this' is a cue to screen early with a validated tool. A positive screen leads to the acuity question: a yes is an acute positive, imminent risk, and the patient cannot leave until evaluated. The nurse keeps him in sight at all times in a cleared room, stores his belongings under the policy, tells the physician at once and hands off to the evaluator, and never asks for a description of a method.
